parts.name: Entrance Chant
parts.when: as the priest and ministers process in
parts.about: The opening song begins the celebration, deepens the unity of the gathered people, draws their minds into the season or feast, and accompanies the procession of the priest and ministers (GIRM 47). It may be the antiphon and psalm from the Roman Missal or Graduale, or another suitable liturgical song (GIRM 48).

parts.name: Kyrie (Lord, Have Mercy)
parts.when: after the Penitential Act, or as part of it
parts.about: A short litany in which the people acclaim the Lord and ask his mercy, usually with each invocation sung twice by cantor and assembly (GIRM 52). Its Greek words are among the oldest in the Roman Mass.

parts.name: Gloria
parts.when: after the Kyrie on Sundays (outside Advent and Lent), solemnities, and feasts
parts.about: An ancient hymn in which the Church, gathered in the Holy Spirit, praises the Father and the Lamb. It is meant to be sung and its text may not be replaced by another song (GIRM 53); it is omitted on the Sundays of Advent and Lent.

parts.name: Responsorial Psalm
parts.about: The psalm is an integral part of the Liturgy of the Word, ideally sung with the people answering a refrain (GIRM 61). It should be the psalm itself as given in the Lectionary or an approved collection, so a loose hymn paraphrase is no substitute; the psalm-based songs listed here are better suited to Communion or to seasonal common psalms where approved.

parts.name: Gospel Acclamation
parts.when: standing, before the Gospel is proclaimed
parts.about: The assembly welcomes the Lord who is about to speak in the Gospel and professes its faith by singing (GIRM 62). The Alleluia is sung in every season except Lent, when another acclamation from the Lectionary takes its place (GIRM 62).

parts.name: Preparation of the Gifts (Offertory)
parts.when: while the bread and wine are brought forward and the altar is prepared
parts.about: A chant may accompany the procession with the gifts and continue until they are placed on the altar (GIRM 74). Unlike the Sanctus or Agnus Dei, its text is not fixed, so hymns and instrumental music are common here.

parts.name: Holy, Holy, Holy (Sanctus)
parts.when: at the end of the Preface of the Eucharistic Prayer
parts.about: The whole assembly joins the angels' song from Isaiah 6 and the crowds' Hosanna from Palm Sunday (GIRM 79b). It is part of the Eucharistic Prayer and is sung by everyone, priest and people together.

parts.name: Mystery of Faith (Memorial Acclamation)
parts.when: after the consecration, when the priest invites it
parts.about: The people proclaim the death and Resurrection of Christ and look to his coming again, using one of the acclamations given in the Roman Missal. Because its texts are fixed, it is sung as part of a Mass setting rather than replaced by a hymn.

parts.name: Great Amen
parts.when: after the doxology that concludes the Eucharistic Prayer
parts.about: The priest offers the final doxology and the people confirm and conclude the whole Eucharistic Prayer with their Amen (GIRM 79h). Many settings stretch it into a festive, repeated acclamation.

parts.name: Lamb of God (Agnus Dei)
parts.when: during the breaking of the bread
parts.about: The invocation accompanies the fraction of the consecrated bread and may be repeated as long as the breaking continues, always ending with the plea for peace (GIRM 83).

parts.name: Communion Chant
parts.when: while the priest and people receive Communion
parts.about: The singing expresses the communicants' unity of voice and heart and highlights the communal character of the procession (GIRM 86). It begins when the priest receives and may be the Missal or Graduale antiphon, a psalm, or another suitable song (GIRM 87); a hymn of praise may follow once all have received (GIRM 88).

parts.name: Recessional (Closing Song)
parts.when: as the priest and ministers leave
parts.about: The General Instruction of the Roman Missal does not prescribe a closing hymn: the Mass ends with the dismissal, and the ministers then reverence the altar and withdraw (GIRM 90). A closing hymn or organ music is a widespread custom in the United States rather than a required part of the rite.

seasons.name: Advent
seasons.about: The four weeks of expectant preparation before Christmas. The Gloria is omitted on the Sundays of Advent, and music is meant to be more restrained than at Christmas, so the full joy of the feast is not anticipated.

seasons.name: Christmas
seasons.about: From the Vigil of Christmas through the Baptism of the Lord, including the Holy Family, Mary Mother of God, and the Epiphany. Carols that stayed quiet in Advent come into their own.

seasons.name: Lent
seasons.about: The forty days from Ash Wednesday leading to the Easter Triduum. The Gloria is omitted and the Alleluia is not sung at all until the Easter Vigil, and instruments are used more sparingly.

seasons.name: Holy Week
seasons.about: From Palm Sunday through the Sacred Paschal Triduum: the Mass of the Lord's Supper, Good Friday, and the Easter Vigil. Each day has its own distinctive chants, from the Palm Sunday Hosannas to the Exsultet.

seasons.name: Easter
seasons.about: The fifty days from Easter Sunday to Pentecost, celebrated as one great feast. The Alleluia returns and the Gloria is sung on every Sunday.

seasons.name: Pentecost
seasons.about: The close of the Easter season, celebrating the outpouring of the Holy Spirit; the Sequence Veni Sancte Spiritus is sung before the Gospel on Pentecost Sunday. These songs also suit Confirmation.

seasons.name: Ordinary Time
seasons.about: The 'counted' weeks of the year outside the major seasons, when the Church follows the public ministry of Christ. A broad repertoire of hymns of praise, discipleship, and mission fits here.

seasons.name: Marian Feasts
seasons.about: Songs honoring the Blessed Virgin Mary for her solemnities and feasts, for May and October devotions, and for the seasonal Marian antiphons sung after Night Prayer.

seasons.name: Eucharistic Adoration
seasons.about: Songs for Exposition and Benediction of the Blessed Sacrament, Holy Hours, and Corpus Christi processions. The Tantum Ergo is traditionally sung before the blessing at Benediction.

seasons.name: Funerals
seasons.about: Songs for the Order of Christian Funerals, which express both grief and hope in the Resurrection. The In Paradisum is the traditional chant as the body is carried from the church.

seasons.name: Weddings
seasons.about: Songs suited to a Catholic wedding, whether celebrated within Mass or not. Music should be sacred rather than secular; check parish guidelines, which often have a list.

seasons.name: Feasts of Saints
seasons.about: Songs for All Saints' Day, the feasts of particular saints, and occasions that celebrate the communion of saints.

songs.title: Kyrie (Mass VIII, de Angelis)
songs.composer: Gregorian chant (Mass VIII, melody c. 15th–16th century)
songs.textAuthor: Traditional Latin liturgical text (Greek words, in use in the Roman Mass since antiquity)
translation: Lord, have mercy.
Lord, have mercy.
Lord, have mercy.
Christ, have mercy.
Christ, have mercy.
Christ, have mercy.
Lord, have mercy.
Lord, have mercy.
Lord, have mercy.
songs.about: The Kyrie is one of the few Greek texts kept in the Latin Mass, a cry for mercy addressed to Christ. The 'de Angelis' setting is the best-known Gregorian Mass in the United States and is often the first chant Mass a parish learns.

songs.title: Gloria (Mass VIII, de Angelis)
songs.textAuthor: Traditional Latin liturgical text (ancient Christian hymn, in the Roman Mass since the early Middle Ages)
lyrics: et in terra pax hominibus bonae voluntatis.
gratias agimus tibi propter magnam gloriam tuam,
Domine Deus, Agnus Dei, Filius Patris,
qui tollis peccata mundi, miserere nobis;
qui tollis peccata mundi, suscipe deprecationem nostram.
Qui sedes ad dexteram Patris, miserere nobis.
Quoniam tu solus Sanctus, tu solus Dominus,
cum Sancto Spiritu: in gloria Dei Patris.
translation: Glory be to God on high,
and peace on earth to people whom he favors.
You we praise, you we bless,
you we worship, you we glorify;
we thank you for the greatness of your glory,
O Lord God, King of heaven,
God the Father, ruler of all.
O Lord, only-begotten Son, Jesus Christ,
Lord God, Lamb of God, the Father's Son,
you take away the world's sins: show us mercy;
you take away the world's sins: take up our plea.
You are seated at the Father's right hand: show us mercy.
For you alone are the Holy One, you alone the Lord,
you alone the Most High, Jesus Christ,
together with the Holy Spirit, in the glory of God the Father.
Amen.
songs.about: The Gloria opens with the angels' song at Bethlehem and grows into a hymn to the Father and to Christ the Lamb. It is sung on Sundays outside Advent and Lent and on solemnities and feasts.

songs.title: Sanctus (Mass VIII, de Angelis)
lyrics: Pleni sunt caeli et terra gloria tua.
Benedictus qui venit in nomine Domini.
translation: Holy, holy, holy
is the Lord, the God of hosts.
Heaven and earth are filled with your glory.
Hosanna in the heights.
Blessed is the one who comes in the Lord's name.
Hosanna in the heights.
songs.about: The Sanctus joins the seraphim's cry from Isaiah's vision to the crowd's welcome of Jesus into Jerusalem. It is sung by the whole assembly at the end of the Preface, as the Eucharistic Prayer begins.

songs.title: Agnus Dei (Mass VIII, de Angelis)
songs.textAuthor: Traditional Latin liturgical text (added to the Roman Mass c. 700)
lyrics: Agnus Dei, qui tollis peccata mundi: miserere nobis.
Agnus Dei, qui tollis peccata mundi: miserere nobis.
Agnus Dei, qui tollis peccata mundi: dona nobis pacem.
translation: Lamb of God, you who take away the world's sins: show us mercy.
Lamb of God, you who take away the world's sins: show us mercy.
Lamb of God, you who take away the world's sins: give us peace.
songs.about: The Agnus Dei echoes John the Baptist pointing to Jesus as the Lamb of God. It accompanies the breaking of the consecrated Host, and may be repeated as long as the fraction lasts, always ending with the plea for peace.

songs.title: Kyrie (Mass XVIII)
lyrics: Kyrie, eleison. Kyrie, eleison. Kyrie, eleison.
Christe, eleison. Christe, eleison. Christe, eleison.
Kyrie, eleison. Kyrie, eleison. Kyrie, eleison.
translation: Lord, have mercy (three times).
Christ, have mercy (three times).
Lord, have mercy (three times).
songs.about: Mass XVIII is the simplest chant Ordinary in the Roman Gradual, traditionally used on weekdays of Advent and Lent and at Masses for the dead. Its narrow, almost spoken melody suits penitential seasons.

songs.title: Sanctus (Mass XVIII)
lyrics: Pleni sunt caeli et terra gloria tua.
Benedictus qui venit in nomine Domini.
translation: Holy, holy, holy
is the Lord, the God of hosts.
Heaven and earth are filled with your glory.
Hosanna in the heights.
Blessed is the one who comes in the Lord's name.
Hosanna in the heights.
songs.about: A very simple chant Sanctus, close to a recitation tone, that any congregation can learn in one hearing. It appears in the US Roman Missal's chant appendix and many parish worship aids.

songs.title: Agnus Dei (Mass XVIII)
lyrics: Agnus Dei, qui tollis peccata mundi: miserere nobis.
Agnus Dei, qui tollis peccata mundi: miserere nobis.
Agnus Dei, qui tollis peccata mundi: dona nobis pacem.
translation: Lamb of God, you who take away the world's sins: show us mercy.
Lamb of God, you who take away the world's sins: show us mercy.
Lamb of God, you who take away the world's sins: give us peace.
songs.about: The plain-chant Agnus Dei of Mass XVIII, often paired with its Sanctus during Advent and Lent. Its simplicity makes it a good first Latin chant for a congregation.

songs.title: The Lord's Prayer (chant)
lyrics: Pater noster, qui es in caelis,
Fiat voluntas tua, sicut in caelo et in terra.
Panem nostrum cotidianum da nobis hodie,
sicut et nos dimittimus debitoribus nostris.
Et ne nos inducas in tentationem;
translation: Our Father, you who are in the heavens,
may your name be held holy.
May your kingdom come.
May your will be done, on earth as in heaven.
Give us today our daily bread,
and release us from our debts,
just as we release those indebted to us.
And do not bring us into testing,
but deliver us from evil.
songs.about: The prayer Jesus taught his disciples, sung by priest and people together before Communion. The Latin chant tone printed in the Roman Missal is short and widely known; the traditional English Our Father is also commonly sung to a melody adapted from it.

songs.title: Creed (Credo III)
lyrics: Patrem omnipotentem, factorem caeli et terrae,
Et in unum Dominum Iesum Christum,
et ex Patre natum ante omnia saecula.
Deum de Deo, lumen de lumine, Deum verum de Deo vero,
Qui propter nos homines et propter nostram salutem
Et incarnatus est de Spiritu Sancto
ex Maria Virgine, et homo factus est.
Crucifixus etiam pro nobis sub Pontio Pilato;
et resurrexit tertia die, secundum Scripturas,
et ascendit in caelum, sedet ad dexteram Patris.
Et iterum venturus est cum gloria,
Et in Spiritum Sanctum, Dominum et vivificantem:
Qui cum Patre et Filio simul adoratur et conglorificatur:
Et unam, sanctam, catholicam et apostolicam Ecclesiam.
Confiteor unum baptisma in remissionem peccatorum.
translation: I believe in a single God,
the Father, all-powerful, who made sky and earth
and everything, seen and unseen.
And in a single Lord, Jesus Christ,
God's one and only Son,
born of the Father before all ages:
God out of God, light out of light, true God out of true God,
begotten and not made, sharing one being with the Father;
through him everything came to be.
For us humans and for our rescue
he came down from heaven,
and by the Holy Spirit he took flesh
from the Virgin Mary, and became a man.
For our sake he was also crucified under Pontius Pilate;
he suffered and was buried,
and on the third day he rose, as the Scriptures had said,
and went up into heaven, and sits at the Father's right hand.
He will come again in glory
to judge the living and the dead,
and his reign will have no end.
And in the Holy Spirit, Lord and life-giver,
who comes forth from the Father and the Son,
who is worshiped and glorified together with Father and Son,
who spoke through the prophets.
And in one, holy, catholic and apostolic Church.
I acknowledge one baptism for sins to be forgiven.
And I await the rising of the dead
and the life of the age to come.
Amen.
songs.about: The Creed of Nicaea and Constantinople, professed on Sundays and solemnities after the homily. Credo III, a later Gregorian melody, is the chant setting most parishes know; the creed may be sung or recited.

songs.title: Through Him (Final Doxology)
songs.textAuthor: Traditional Latin liturgical text (conclusion of the ancient Roman Canon)
lyrics: Per ipsum, et cum ipso, et in ipso,
translation: Through him, and with him, and in him,
to you, God the all-powerful Father,
in the unity of the Holy Spirit,
belongs all honor and glory
through every age of ages.
Amen.
songs.about: The priest sings this doxology while raising the Body and Blood of Christ at the end of the Eucharistic Prayer; the people answer with the Great Amen. Only the priest sings the doxology itself; the Amen belongs to everyone.

songs.title: Hail, Holy Queen
songs.composer: Gregorian chant (simple tone, 17th century; solemn tone medieval)
songs.textAuthor: Traditional Latin liturgical text (11th century, often attributed to Hermann of Reichenau)
lyrics: vita, dulcedo, et spes nostra, salve.
Ad te clamamus, exsules filii Evae.
Ad te suspiramus, gementes et flentes
illos tuos misericordes oculos ad nos converte.
Et Iesum, benedictum fructum ventris tui,
O clemens, O pia, O dulcis Virgo Maria.
translation: Hail, Queen, mother of mercy,
our life, our sweetness and our hope, hail.
To you we cry out, exiled children of Eve.
To you we sigh, mourning and weeping
in this valley of tears.
Come then, our advocate,
turn those merciful eyes of yours toward us.
And after this exile show us Jesus,
the blessed fruit of your womb.
O gentle, O loving, O sweet Virgin Mary.
songs.about: The best known of the four seasonal Marian antiphons, sung at the end of Night Prayer from after Pentecost until Advent. Many parishes sing it after the last Mass of the day, at funerals of priests and religious, and at the close of the Rosary.

songs.title: Queen of Heaven, Rejoice
songs.textAuthor: Traditional Latin liturgical text (12th century or earlier)
translation: Queen of heaven, rejoice, alleluia.
For he whom you were worthy to carry, alleluia,
has risen, as he said, alleluia.
Pray to God for us, alleluia.
songs.about: The Easter Marian antiphon, sung from the Easter Vigil until Pentecost; during those weeks it also replaces the Angelus. Its four short lines congratulate Mary on her Son's resurrection.

songs.title: Loving Mother of the Redeemer
songs.textAuthor: Traditional Latin liturgical text (11th century, often attributed to Hermann of Reichenau)
lyrics: Alma Redemptoris Mater, quae pervia caeli
porta manes, et stella maris, succurre cadenti,
Gabrielis ab ore sumens illud Ave,
translation: Loving Mother of the Redeemer, you who remain heaven's
open gate and star of the sea, come to the aid of a falling people
who strive to rise again:
you who, while nature marveled,
gave birth to your own holy Creator,
a virgin before and after,
who heard that 'Ave' from Gabriel's lips,
have mercy on sinners.
songs.about: The Marian antiphon of Advent and Christmastide, sung from the First Sunday of Advent until the Presentation of the Lord (February 2). It recalls the Annunciation and Mary's virginal motherhood.

songs.title: Hail, Queen of Heaven
songs.textAuthor: Traditional Latin liturgical text (12th century or earlier)
lyrics: ex qua mundo lux est orta.
translation: Hail, Queen of the heavens,
hail, Lady of the angels:
hail, root, hail, gate,
from which light has dawned on the world.
Rejoice, glorious Virgin,
lovely beyond all others;
farewell, O most beautiful,
and plead with Christ for us.
songs.about: The Marian antiphon from February 2 until Holy Thursday, so it is the one heard through Lent. It greets Mary as the 'root' of Jesse and the gate through which Christ the light entered the world.

songs.title: Hail Mary (chant)
songs.composer: Gregorian chant (offertory/antiphon melodies); famous later settings by Schubert, Bach–Gounod and Victoria
songs.textAuthor: Traditional Latin liturgical text (Luke 1:28, 1:42; petition in use by the 16th century)
lyrics: et benedictus fructus ventris tui, Iesus.
nunc et in hora mortis nostrae.
translation: Hail Mary, full of grace,
the Lord is with you.
You are blessed among women,
and blessed is the fruit of your womb, Jesus.
Holy Mary, Mother of God,
pray for us sinners,
now and at the hour of our death.
Amen.
songs.about: The angel's greeting and Elizabeth's blessing, followed by the Church's petition. Beyond the chant, the Latin text is often sung as a solo at weddings (frequently while the couple honors Mary) and at funerals in the settings by Schubert or Bach–Gounod.

songs.title: Hail, Star of the Sea
songs.textAuthor: Traditional Latin liturgical text (hymn, 9th century or earlier)
translation: Hail, star of the sea,
nurturing Mother of God,
and Virgin for ever,
happy gate of heaven.
Receiving that 'Ave'
from Gabriel's mouth,
settle us in peace,
reversing the name of 'Eva'.
Loosen the chains of the guilty,
bring light to the blind,
drive away our evils,
ask for every good.
Show yourself a mother;
through you may he receive our prayers
who, born for our sake,
chose to be your own.
Virgin without equal,
gentlest of all,
free us from our faults
and make us gentle and chaste.
Grant us a pure life,
prepare a safe road,
so that, seeing Jesus,
we may rejoice together for ever.
Praise be to God the Father,
glory to Christ most high,
and to the Holy Spirit:
to the three, one honor. Amen.
songs.about: An ancient Vespers hymn for Marian feasts. The second verse plays on the reversal of 'Eva' into 'Ave', Mary undoing Eve's disobedience.

songs.title: We Fly to Thy Protection
songs.textAuthor: Traditional Latin liturgical text (from a Greek prayer known on a papyrus of the 3rd–4th century)
lyrics: sed a periculis cunctis libera nos semper,
translation: Under your protection we take refuge,
holy Mother of God.
Do not disregard our pleas
in our needs,
but always free us from every danger,
glorious and blessed Virgin.
songs.about: The oldest known prayer to Mary outside Scripture. It is a short, quiet antiphon suited to the end of a Marian devotion or a weekday Mass.

songs.title: O Most Holy
songs.composer: Traditional melody (often called the 'Sicilian Mariners' Hymn', printed in the 1790s)
songs.textAuthor: Traditional Latin liturgical text (Marian hymn, 18th century)
translation: O most holy, O most loving,
sweet Virgin Mary!
Beloved Mother, undefiled,
pray, pray for us.
songs.about: A short, singable Latin hymn to Mary on a lilting tune, a favorite for May devotions and Marian processions.

songs.title: Canticle of Mary
songs.composer: Gregorian chant (psalm tones); countless polyphonic settings
lyrics: et exsultavit spiritus meus in Deo salutari meo,
Ecce enim ex hoc beatam me dicent omnes generationes,
quia fecit mihi magna, qui potens est,
et misericordia eius in progenies et progenies
sicut locutus est ad patres nostros,
Abraham et semini eius in saecula.
translation: My soul declares the greatness of the Lord,
and my spirit leaps for joy in God my Savior,
for he has looked on his servant in her lowliness.
From now on every generation will call me blessed,
for the Mighty One has done great things for me,
and holy is his name,
and his mercy reaches from generation to generation
to those who fear him.
He has shown the strength of his arm,
he has scattered those proud in their hearts' thoughts;
he has pulled the powerful from their thrones
and lifted up the lowly.
The hungry he has filled with good things,
and the rich he has sent away empty.
He has taken up the cause of Israel his servant,
remembering his mercy,
as he promised our fathers,
Abraham and his descendants for ever.
songs.about: Mary's song at the Visitation, sung every evening at Vespers. At Mass it is a fitting song of thanksgiving after Communion, especially on Marian feasts and in late Advent.

songs.title: Hail, True Body
songs.composer: Gregorian chant; best-known setting by Mozart (K. 618, 1791)
songs.textAuthor: Traditional Latin liturgical text (14th-century Eucharistic hymn)
lyrics: O Iesu dulcis, O Iesu pie,
translation: Hail, true body, born
of the Virgin Mary,
that truly suffered and was sacrificed
on the cross for humankind,
whose pierced side
flowed with water and blood:
be for us a foretaste
in the trial of death.
O sweet Jesus, O loving Jesus,
O Jesus, son of Mary.
songs.about: A medieval greeting to Christ present in the Eucharist, traditionally sung at the elevation. Mozart's brief, luminous setting is one of the most-sung choral pieces at Communion.

songs.title: Bread of Angels
songs.composer: Chant; famous setting by César Franck (1872)
songs.textAuthor: St. Thomas Aquinas (1264), Traditional Latin liturgical text (from the hymn Sacris solemniis)
translation: The bread of angels
becomes the bread of humans;
the bread of heaven
brings the old foreshadowings to an end.
O wondrous thing!
The poor, the servant and the lowly
feed upon their Lord.
Godhead, three and one,
this we beg of you:
visit us
as we worship you;
by your paths
lead us where we are heading,
to the light in which you dwell. Amen.
songs.about: Two stanzas from a hymn St. Thomas Aquinas wrote for the new feast of Corpus Christi. Franck's setting for solo voice is a perennial choice at Communion during weddings and First Communions.

songs.title: Down in Adoration Falling
songs.textAuthor: St. Thomas Aquinas (1264), Traditional Latin liturgical text (last two stanzas of Pange lingua)
translation: So great a Sacrament, therefore,
let us revere, bowing low;
and let the old instruction
give way to the new rite;
let faith provide what is lacking
where the senses fail.
To the Father and the Son
be praise and jubilation,
salvation, honor, power too,
and blessing;
to the One proceeding from them both
be equal praise. Amen.
songs.about: Sung at every Benediction before the priest blesses the people with the Monstrance, and at the transfer of the Blessed Sacrament on Holy Thursday. It closes Aquinas's Pange lingua.

songs.title: O Saving Victim
songs.textAuthor: St. Thomas Aquinas (1264), Traditional Latin liturgical text (last two stanzas of Verbum supernum prodiens)
translation: O saving Victim,
who open wide the door of heaven:
hostile wars press hard on us;
give strength, bring help.
To the Lord, one and three,
be glory without end;
may he give us life without limit
in our homeland. Amen.
songs.about: Traditionally sung as the Blessed Sacrament is placed in the Monstrance at the start of Exposition. With Tantum ergo it frames nearly every Holy Hour in the United States.

songs.title: Sing, My Tongue, the Savior's Glory
songs.textAuthor: St. Thomas Aquinas (1264), Traditional Latin liturgical text
translation: Sing, my tongue, the mystery
of the glorious Body
and of the precious Blood
which the King of the nations,
fruit of a noble womb,
poured out as the world's ransom.
Given to us, born for us
of a spotless Virgin,
he lived in the world,
scattering the seed of the word,
and closed his time among us
in a wondrous way.
On the night of the Last Supper,
reclining with his brothers,
having kept the law in full
with the foods it required,
he gives himself with his own hands
as food for the Twelve.
The Word made flesh, by his word,
makes true bread into his flesh,
and wine becomes the blood of Christ;
and if the senses fail,
faith alone is enough
to make a sincere heart firm.
So great a Sacrament, therefore,
let us revere, bowing low;
and let the old instruction
give way to the new rite;
let faith provide what is lacking
where the senses fail.
To the Father and the Son
be praise and jubilation,
salvation, honor, power too,
and blessing;
to the One proceeding from them both
be equal praise. Amen.
songs.about: Aquinas's hymn for Corpus Christi, sung above all at the end of the Mass of the Lord's Supper on Holy Thursday, as the Blessed Sacrament is carried to the altar of repose.

songs.title: Godhead Here in Hiding
songs.textAuthor: Attributed to St. Thomas Aquinas (13th century), Traditional Latin liturgical text
lyrics: quae sub his figuris vere latitas:
tibi se cor meum totum subicit,
Visus, tactus, gustus in te fallitur,
at hic latet simul et humanitas;
fac me tibi semper magis credere,
in te spem habere, te diligere.
praesta meae menti de te vivere
et te illi semper dulce sapere.
totum mundum quit ab omni scelere.
oro fiat illud quod tam sitio:
visu sim beatus tuae gloriae. Amen.
translation: I adore you with devotion, hidden Godhead,
truly hidden beneath these forms:
my whole heart submits itself to you,
for in contemplating you it fails entirely.
Sight, touch and taste are deceived in you,
but hearing alone is safely believed;
I believe whatever the Son of God has said:
nothing is truer than this word of Truth.
On the cross the Godhead alone was hidden,
but here the humanity is hidden too;
yet believing and confessing both,
I ask what the repentant thief asked.
I do not see the wounds, as Thomas did,
yet I confess you are my God;
make me always believe in you more,
hope in you, and love you.
O memorial of the Lord's death!
Living bread that gives life to humankind!
Grant my mind to live on you
and always to find you sweet.
Loving pelican, Lord Jesus,
cleanse me, unclean, with your blood,
of which one drop could save
the whole world from all its sin.
Jesus, whom I now see veiled,
I pray that what I thirst for may come to pass:
that seeing your face unveiled,
I may be happy in the sight of your glory. Amen.
songs.about: A personal meditation on Christ's hidden presence in the Eucharist, moving from doubting Thomas and the good thief to the hope of seeing God face to face. It is sung during Adoration and as a quiet Communion hymn.

songs.title: Praise, O Zion (Corpus Christi Sequence)
songs.textAuthor: St. Thomas Aquinas (1264), Traditional Latin liturgical text (selected stanzas)
lyrics: Tu, qui cuncta scis et vales,
translation: Praise, O Zion, your Savior,
praise your leader and shepherd
in hymns and songs.
Dare as much as you can:
for he is greater than all praise,
and you can never praise him enough.
Behold the bread of angels,
made food for travelers:
truly the children's bread,
not to be thrown to dogs.
Good shepherd, true bread,
Jesus, have mercy on us:
feed us, protect us,
let us see good things
in the land of the living.
You who know and can do all things,
who feed us mortals here:
make us your table-companions there,
co-heirs and comrades
of the holy citizens. Amen. Alleluia.
songs.about: The optional Sequence for the Solemnity of the Most Holy Body and Blood of Christ, sung before the Alleluia. The full text has 24 stanzas; the Missal permits the short form beginning 'Ecce panis angelorum'.

songs.title: Where Charity and Love Are
songs.textAuthor: Traditional Latin liturgical text (antiphon for the Holy Thursday foot-washing, c. 8th century)
lyrics: Ubi caritas et amor, Deus ibi est.
Congregavit nos in unum Christi amor.
Et ex corde diligamus nos sincero.
Simul ergo cum in unum congregamur:
Et in medio nostri sit Christus Deus.
gaudium, quod est immensum atque probum,
translation: Where charity and love are, God is there.
The love of Christ has gathered us into one.
Let us rejoice and be glad in him.
Let us fear and love the living God.
And let us love one another with a sincere heart.
So when we are gathered together as one,
let us take care not to be divided in mind.
Let spiteful quarrels cease, let disputes end.
And in our midst let Christ our God be present.
And with the blessed may we also see
your face in glory, O Christ our God:
a joy that is immense and good,
through endless ages of ages. Amen.
songs.about: Sung during or after the washing of feet and at the presentation of gifts on Holy Thursday; the current Missal gives the refrain as 'Ubi caritas est vera' ('where charity is true'). Its theme of love and unity also makes it a favorite at weddings.

songs.title: Hear Us, O Lord
songs.textAuthor: Traditional Latin liturgical text (Mozarabic origin, selected stanzas)
lyrics: Ad te Rex summe, omnium Redemptor,
translation: Listen, O Lord, and have mercy,
for we have sinned against you.
To you, highest King, Redeemer of all,
we lift our weeping eyes:
hear, O Christ, the prayers of those who plead.
Right hand of the Father, cornerstone,
way of salvation, gate of heaven,
wash away the stains of our sin.
songs.about: A penitential litany whose refrain asks God to hear and pity his sinful people. It is the classic Lenten entrance or penitential song in Latin.

songs.title: Spare, O Lord
translation: Spare, O Lord, spare your people:
do not be angry with us for ever.
songs.about: A short refrain built on the prophet Joel's call to the priests to weep between porch and altar; Joel 2 is also read on Ash Wednesday. It is often sung during the distribution of ashes and throughout Lent, alternating with penitential verses.

songs.title: At the Cross Her Station Keeping (Latin)
songs.composer: Gregorian chant (and settings by Pergolesi, Palestrina, Rossini and others)
songs.textAuthor: Attributed to Jacopone da Todi (13th century), Traditional Latin liturgical text (selected stanzas)
translation: The sorrowing Mother stood
in tears beside the cross
while her Son hung there.
Through her soul, groaning,
saddened and grieving,
a sword had passed.
O how sad and stricken
was that blessed one,
mother of the Only-begotten!
She mourned and grieved,
the loving Mother, as she saw
the torments of her glorious Son.
Come, Mother, fountain of love,
make me feel the force of your sorrow,
so that I may mourn with you.
Make my heart burn
with love for Christ my God,
so that I may please him.
When my body dies,
grant that my soul be given
the glory of paradise. Amen.
songs.about: A medieval meditation on Mary at the foot of the cross. It is the optional Sequence for Our Lady of Sorrows (September 15) and is traditionally sung between the Stations of the Cross.

songs.title: The Royal Banners Forward Go (Latin)
songs.textAuthor: Venantius Fortunatus (569), Traditional Latin liturgical text (first and penultimate stanzas)
translation: The banners of the King go forth,
the mystery of the Cross shines out,
on which the maker of flesh, in the flesh,
was hung upon the gallows.
Hail, O Cross, our only hope!
In this season of the Passion
increase grace for the faithful
and blot out the sins of the guilty.
songs.about: Written for the arrival of a relic of the True Cross at Poitiers, this hymn is sung at Vespers in Holy Week and on the Exaltation of the Cross (September 14). The 'O Crux, ave' stanza is often sung on its own.

songs.title: Faithful Cross
songs.textAuthor: Venantius Fortunatus (6th century), Traditional Latin liturgical text (refrain of Pange lingua gloriosi proelium)
translation: Faithful Cross, the one noble tree
among all the trees:
no forest brings forth its like
in flower, leaf or bud.
Sweet wood, with sweet nails,
bearing a sweet weight.
songs.about: The refrain of the great hymn sung during the Adoration of the Cross on Good Friday. It praises the wood of the cross as the tree of life.

songs.title: Hosanna to the Son of David
lyrics: benedictus qui venit in nomine Domini.
translation: Hosanna to the Son of David:
blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.
O King of Israel:
Hosanna in the highest.
songs.about: The first antiphon given in the Missal for the blessing of palms on Palm Sunday, taken from the Gospel of the Lord's entry into Jerusalem.

songs.title: The Children of the Hebrews
translation: The children of the Hebrews, carrying olive branches,
went out to meet the Lord, crying out and saying:
Hosanna in the highest.
songs.about: One of the Palm Sunday processional antiphons, traditionally sung as the people carry their palms into church.

songs.title: Easter Proclamation (opening)
songs.textAuthor: Traditional Latin liturgical text (Easter Vigil, 7th century or earlier; opening lines only)
translation: Let the angelic host of heaven now rejoice;
let the divine mysteries rejoice;
and for the victory of so great a King
let the trumpet of salvation sound.
songs.about: The long proclamation sung by a deacon or priest beside the paschal candle at the start of the Easter Vigil, after the procession with the acclamation 'Lumen Christi'. Only its opening is given here; the official English text belongs to the Roman Missal and is not reproduced.

songs.title: Christians, to the Paschal Victim (Easter Sequence)
songs.textAuthor: Attributed to Wipo of Burgundy (11th century), Traditional Latin liturgical text
translation: To the Paschal Victim
let Christians offer praise.
The Lamb has ransomed the sheep:
Christ, the innocent one,
has reconciled sinners to the Father.
Death and life have fought
in a wondrous duel:
the leader of life, who died,
now reigns alive.
Tell us, Mary,
what did you see on the way?
I saw the tomb of the living Christ
and the glory of his rising:
the angel witnesses,
the face-cloth and the linens.
Christ my hope has risen:
he will go before his own into Galilee.
We know that Christ has truly risen
from the dead:
O victorious King, have mercy on us.
Amen. Alleluia.
songs.about: The Easter Sequence, required on Easter Sunday and optional through the Octave; it is sung before the Alleluia. It stages a short dialogue with Mary Magdalene, the first witness of the empty tomb.

songs.title: I Saw Water Flowing
lyrics: et omnes ad quos pervenit aqua ista
salvi facti sunt, et dicent: alleluia, alleluia.
translation: I saw water flowing out from the temple,
from its right side, alleluia:
and all those whom this water reached
were saved, and they will say: alleluia, alleluia.
songs.about: The antiphon for the sprinkling rite with blessed water during Easter Time, which may replace the Penitential Act on Sundays. It reads Ezekiel's river from the Temple as the water of baptism flowing from Christ's side.

songs.title: Sprinkle Me, O Lord
lyrics: Asperges me, Domine, hyssopo, et mundabor:
lavabis me, et super nivem dealbabor.
translation: Sprinkle me, O Lord, with hyssop, and I shall be clean:
wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow.
Have mercy on me, O God,
according to your great mercy.
songs.about: The traditional antiphon for the Sunday sprinkling rite outside Easter Time, from David's great psalm of repentance. The rite recalls baptism and may take the place of the Penitential Act.

songs.title: Come, Creator Spirit
songs.textAuthor: Attributed to Rabanus Maurus (9th century), Traditional Latin liturgical text
translation: Come, Creator Spirit,
visit the minds of your own,
fill with grace from above
the hearts that you have made.
You who are called the Advocate,
gift of God most high,
living spring, fire, love,
and anointing of the spirit.
Sevenfold in your gifts,
finger of the Father's right hand,
the Father's promise duly kept,
you enrich our throats with speech.
Kindle a light in our senses,
pour love into our hearts,
strengthening the weakness of our bodies
with your lasting power.
Drive the enemy far away
and give us peace at once;
with you going before us as guide
may we avoid all harm.
Grant that through you we may know the Father,
and come to know the Son,
and believe in you, the Spirit of both,
at all times.
Glory be to God the Father,
and to the Son, who rose
from the dead, and to the Advocate,
for ages of ages. Amen.
songs.about: The great hymn to the Holy Spirit, sung at Pentecost, Confirmations, ordinations and the opening of a conclave. It is one of the most widely used hymns in the Latin Church.

songs.title: Come, Holy Spirit (Pentecost Sequence)
songs.textAuthor: Attributed to Stephen Langton (c. 1200), Traditional Latin liturgical text
translation: Come, Holy Spirit,
and send from heaven
a ray of your light.
Come, father of the poor,
come, giver of gifts,
come, light of hearts.
Best of comforters,
sweet guest of the soul,
sweet refreshment.
Rest in labor,
cool in the heat,
solace in tears.
O most blessed light,
fill the inmost hearts
of your faithful.
Without your divine power
there is nothing in us,
nothing that is free of harm.
Wash what is soiled,
water what is dry,
heal what is wounded.
Bend what is rigid,
warm what is cold,
guide what has strayed.
Give to your faithful,
who trust in you,
the sacred sevenfold gifts.
Give the reward of virtue,
give a saving end,
give everlasting joy. Amen. Alleluia.
songs.about: Called the 'Golden Sequence', it is required on Pentecost Sunday, sung before the Alleluia. Each short stanza names a way the Spirit comforts, heals or guides.

songs.title: Drop Down Dew, You Heavens
songs.textAuthor: Traditional Latin liturgical text (Isaiah 45:8 and 64; refrain and first verse)
lyrics: ecce civitas Sancti facta est deserta:
domus sanctificationis tuae et gloriae tuae,
translation: Drop down dew, you heavens, from above,
and let the clouds rain down the Just One.
Do not be angry, O Lord,
remember our wrongdoing no longer:
see, the city of the Holy One has become a wilderness:
Zion has become a wilderness,
Jerusalem lies desolate:
the house of your holiness and your glory,
where our fathers praised you.
songs.about: The Advent chant par excellence, built on Isaiah's longing for the heavens to rain down salvation. Its refrain is also the Entrance Antiphon of the Fourth Sunday of Advent.

songs.title: A Child Is Born to Us
translation: A child is born to us,
and a son is given to us:
whose rule rests on his shoulder;
and his name will be called
Messenger of great counsel.
songs.about: The Gregorian Introit of the Mass during the Day on Christmas. The Vulgate (Greek-based) wording 'Angel of great counsel' differs from modern translations of Isaiah.

songs.title: Today Christ Is Born
songs.composer: Gregorian chant (and polyphonic settings by Sweelinck, Palestrina and others)
songs.textAuthor: Traditional Latin liturgical text (Magnificat antiphon for Christmas Vespers)
translation: Today Christ is born;
today the Savior has appeared;
today on earth the Angels sing
and the Archangels rejoice;
today the just exult, saying:
Glory to God in the highest, alleluia.
songs.about: The antiphon for Mary's Canticle at Evening Prayer on Christmas Day, whose repeated 'today' makes the feast present. It is a favorite for choirs as a prelude or after Communion during the Christmas season.

songs.title: May the Angels Lead You into Paradise
lyrics: in tuo adventu suscipiant te martyres,
et perducant te in civitatem sanctam Ierusalem.
translation: May the Angels lead you into paradise;
at your coming may the martyrs receive you
and bring you into the holy city, Jerusalem.
May the choir of Angels receive you,
and with Lazarus, who once was poor,
may you have eternal rest.
songs.about: Sung as the body is carried from the church at the end of the funeral liturgy. It pictures the angels and martyrs escorting the soul to the heavenly Jerusalem, as the angels carried poor Lazarus to Abraham's side.

songs.title: Eternal Rest
songs.textAuthor: Traditional Latin liturgical text (4 Esdras 2:34-35; Psalm 65)
lyrics: Te decet hymnus, Deus, in Sion,
et tibi reddetur votum in Ierusalem:
translation: Eternal rest grant them, O Lord,
and let perpetual light shine on them.
A hymn befits you, O God, in Zion,
and to you a vow shall be fulfilled in Jerusalem:
hear my prayer;
to you all flesh shall come.
songs.about: The traditional Introit of the Mass for the Dead, which gave the 'Requiem Mass' its name. Its antiphon draws on the non-canonical 4 Esdras; the verse is from Psalm 65.

songs.title: Let Eternal Light Shine
translation: May eternal light shine on them, O Lord,
with your saints for ever,
for you are merciful.
Eternal rest grant them, O Lord,
and let perpetual light shine on them.
songs.about: The traditional Communion antiphon of the Requiem Mass, praying that the departed share the unending light of the saints.

songs.title: Day of Wrath
songs.textAuthor: Attributed to Thomas of Celano (13th century), Traditional Latin liturgical text (selected stanzas)
translation: Day of wrath, that day
will dissolve the world in ashes,
as David and the Sibyl bear witness.
How great a trembling there will be
when the judge is to come
to examine all things strictly!
The trumpet, scattering its wondrous sound
through the tombs of every land,
will summon all before the throne.
Remember, loving Jesus,
that I am the reason for your journey:
do not lose me on that day.
Loving Lord Jesus,
grant them rest. Amen.
songs.about: The medieval Sequence of the Requiem Mass. Since the 1970 reform it is no longer part of the funeral Mass in the ordinary form; it survives as an optional hymn in the Liturgy of the Hours for the last week of Ordinary Time and is still sung in the Extraordinary Form.

songs.title: We Praise You, O God
songs.textAuthor: Traditional Latin liturgical text (4th century; traditionally linked to St. Ambrose and St. Augustine, often attributed to Nicetas of Remesiana)
lyrics: Te Deum laudamus: te Dominum confitemur.
Te aeternum Patrem omnis terra veneratur.
Tibi omnes Angeli, tibi caeli et universae Potestates:
tibi Cherubim et Seraphim incessabili voce proclamant:
Sanctus, Sanctus, Sanctus Dominus Deus Sabaoth.
Pleni sunt caeli et terra maiestatis gloriae tuae.
Te per orbem terrarum sancta confitetur Ecclesia,
venerandum tuum verum et unicum Filium;
Tu ad liberandum suscepturus hominem, non horruisti Virginis uterum.
Tu, devicto mortis aculeo, aperuisti credentibus regna caelorum.
Tu ad dexteram Dei sedes, in gloria Patris.
Te ergo quaesumus, tuis famulis subveni, quos pretioso sanguine redemisti.
Aeterna fac cum sanctis tuis in gloria numerari.
Salvum fac populum tuum, Domine, et benedic hereditati tuae.
Et rege eos, et extolle illos usque in aeternum.
et laudamus nomen tuum in saeculum, et in saeculum saeculi.
Dignare, Domine, die isto sine peccato nos custodire.
Fiat misericordia tua, Domine, super nos, quemadmodum speravimus in te.
In te, Domine, speravi: non confundar in aeternum.
translation: We praise you, O God; we acknowledge you as Lord.
All the earth reveres you, eternal Father.
To you all the Angels, the heavens and all the Powers,
to you the Cherubim and Seraphim cry out with unceasing voice:
Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts.
Heaven and earth are full of the majesty of your glory.
The glorious company of Apostles,
the praiseworthy number of the Prophets,
the white-robed army of Martyrs praise you.
Throughout the whole world the holy Church acknowledges you:
the Father of boundless majesty;
your true and only Son, worthy of worship;
and the Holy Spirit, the Advocate.
You, O Christ, are the King of glory.
You are the everlasting Son of the Father.
To set humankind free, you did not shrink from the Virgin's womb.
Having overcome the sting of death, you opened the kingdom of heaven to believers.
You sit at God's right hand, in the glory of the Father.
We believe that you will come as judge.
So we ask you: help your servants, whom you redeemed with your precious blood.
Make them be numbered with your saints in eternal glory.
Save your people, O Lord, and bless your inheritance.
Govern them and lift them up for ever.
Day by day we bless you,
and we praise your name for ever, for ever and ever.
Be pleased, O Lord, to keep us this day without sin.
Have mercy on us, O Lord, have mercy on us.
Let your mercy, O Lord, be upon us, as we have hoped in you.
In you, O Lord, I have hoped: let me never be put to shame.
songs.about: The Church's great hymn of thanksgiving, sung at the end of the Office of Readings on Sundays and feasts and on solemn occasions such as a papal election, an ordination or the last day of the year. 'Holy God, We Praise Thy Name' is a German paraphrase of it.

songs.title: Christ Conquers
lyrics: Christus vincit! Christus regnat! Christus imperat!
translation: Christ conquers! Christ reigns! Christ commands!
songs.about: The ringing refrain of the Carolingian 'royal acclamations', a litany acclaiming Christ the King and invoking the saints. It is used on the Solemnity of Christ the King, at episcopal Masses and on great processional occasions.

songs.title: Holy God, We Praise Thy Name
songs.composer: GROSSER GOTT, from the Katholisches Gesangbuch (Vienna, c. 1774)
songs.textAuthor: Ignaz Franz (German, c. 1771); English by Clarence A. Walworth (1858)
songs.about: A German paraphrase of the ancient Te Deum, carried into English by an American Redemptorist-turned-Paulist priest. It is one of the most-sung processional hymns in American parishes, especially on solemn occasions.

songs.title: Immaculate Mary
songs.composer: LOURDES HYMN, traditional French pilgrimage melody (Grenoble, 1882)
songs.textAuthor: Traditional Lourdes pilgrimage hymn; English versions vary by hymnal
songs.about: The hymn of the candlelight processions at Lourdes, whose refrain is a simple Ave. American parishes sing it on the Immaculate Conception (the patronal feast of the United States) and throughout May and October.

songs.title: O Sacred Head Surrounded
songs.composer: PASSION CHORALE, Hans Leo Hassler (1601); harmonized by J. S. Bach
songs.textAuthor: Medieval Latin poem (attributed to Arnulf of Leuven, formerly to Bernard of Clairvaux); German by Paul Gerhardt (1656); English by Henry W. Baker (1861)
songs.about: A meditation addressed to the wounded face of Christ, passed from Latin to German to English over five centuries. Bach used the melody repeatedly in his St. Matthew Passion, and it remains a staple of Good Friday.

songs.title: Silent Night
songs.textAuthor: Joseph Mohr (German, 1816); English by John Freeman Young (1859)
songs.about: First sung on Christmas Eve 1818 at St. Nicholas Church in Oberndorf, Austria, by its young assistant priest and the parish organist, with guitar accompaniment. It is often sung by candlelight at the close of Christmas Midnight Mass.

songs.title: O Come, All Ye Faithful
songs.composer: ADESTE FIDELES, attributed to John Francis Wade (c. 1743)
songs.textAuthor: Latin, attributed to John Francis Wade; English by Frederick Oakeley (1841)
songs.about: An invitation to come to Bethlehem and adore the newborn King, preserved in manuscripts copied by an English Catholic layman in exile in France. Oakeley, who translated it, later followed John Henry Newman into the Catholic Church.

songs.title: O Come, O Come, Emmanuel
songs.composer: VENI EMMANUEL, adapted from a 15th-century French processional (arr. Thomas Helmore, 1856)
songs.textAuthor: Latin hymn based on the medieval 'O Antiphons' (Cologne, 1710); English by John Mason Neale (1851)
songs.about: Each verse takes up one of the 'O Antiphons' the Church sings at Vespers from December 17 to 23, calling on Christ by an Old Testament title. It is the signature hymn of Advent.

songs.title: Hark! The Herald Angels Sing
songs.composer: MENDELSSOHN, Felix Mendelssohn (1840), adapted by William H. Cummings (1855)
songs.textAuthor: Charles Wesley (1739), altered by George Whitefield and others
songs.about: A Methodist hymn that packs much of the doctrine of the Incarnation into its verses. The tune comes from a cantata Mendelssohn wrote to honor Gutenberg and the printing press.

songs.title: Joy to the World
songs.textAuthor: Isaac Watts (1719), a paraphrase of Psalm 98
songs.about: Watts wrote it as a psalm paraphrase about the Lord's coming to reign, not specifically as a Christmas carol. It has become one of the most familiar recessional hymns of the Christmas season.

songs.title: Angels We Have Heard on High
songs.textAuthor: French carol 'Les anges dans nos campagnes' (18th century); English by James Chadwick (1862)
songs.about: Its famous long-held refrain sets the Latin words the angels sang to the shepherds, the same words that open the Gloria of the Mass. The English version was made by a Catholic bishop of Hexham and Newcastle.

songs.title: What Child Is This
songs.about: Dix set his reflective question-and-answer poem to the old English tune Greensleeves. It is often sung at the preparation of the gifts during the Christmas season and on Epiphany.

songs.title: Faith of Our Fathers
songs.composer: ST. CATHERINE, Henri F. Hemy (1864), adapted by James G. Walton (1874)
songs.about: Faber, an Oratorian convert, wrote it in honor of the English Catholics who kept the faith through penal times and martyrdom. It became a beloved anthem of American Catholic identity.

songs.title: Holy, Holy, Holy! Lord God Almighty
songs.about: Written for Trinity Sunday, it draws on the vision of the heavenly throne room in Revelation 4. The tune is named for the Council of Nicaea, which defended the doctrine of the Trinity.

songs.title: Come, Holy Ghost, Creator Blest
songs.textAuthor: Latin hymn attributed to Rabanus Maurus (9th century); English by Edward Caswall (1849)
songs.about: An English version of the ancient Veni Creator Spiritus, sung to a melody by a French Jesuit. It is a traditional choice at Confirmation, Pentecost, and the start of a school year.

songs.title: Christ the Lord Is Risen Today
songs.about: Wesley's Easter hymn punctuates each line with an Alleluia. It shares its usual tune with 'Jesus Christ Is Risen Today,' and the two are sometimes confused.

songs.title: Jesus Christ Is Risen Today
songs.textAuthor: 14th-century Latin carol; English in Lyra Davidica (1708), with a later stanza by Charles Wesley
songs.about: One of the most-sung Easter hymns in the English-speaking world, descended from a medieval Latin carol. Its soaring Alleluias make it a natural opening or closing hymn on Easter Sunday.

songs.title: The Strife Is O'er
songs.composer: VICTORY, adapted by William H. Monk (1861) from a Gloria Patri by Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina (1591)
songs.textAuthor: Latin hymn (Symphonia Sirenum, Cologne, 1695); English by Francis Pott (1861)
songs.about: A hymn of Christ's victory over death, framed by triple Alleluias. Its melody was adapted from a piece by Palestrina, the great composer of Renaissance church music.

songs.title: Crown Him with Many Crowns
songs.textAuthor: Matthew Bridges (1851), with stanzas by Godfrey Thring (1874)
songs.about: Bridges, an Anglican who became a Catholic, built the hymn on the image of the many crowns of the Rider in Revelation 19. It is a favorite for the Solemnity of Christ the King and the Easter season.

songs.title: Praise to the Lord, the Almighty
songs.composer: LOBE DEN HERREN, from the Stralsund Gesangbuch (1665)
songs.textAuthor: Joachim Neander (German, 1680); English by Catherine Winkworth (1863)
songs.about: A German hymn of praise drawing on Psalms 103 and 150, given its classic English form by Catherine Winkworth. A strong, stately opening hymn for Ordinary Time.

songs.title: Now Thank We All Our God
songs.textAuthor: Martin Rinkart (German, c. 1636); English by Catherine Winkworth (1858)
songs.about: Written by a pastor who ministered through the Thirty Years' War and a deadly plague, it draws on Sirach 50. In the United States it is a natural choice for Thanksgiving Day.

songs.title: All Creatures of Our God and King
songs.composer: LASST UNS ERFREUEN, from Geistliche Kirchengesäng (Cologne, 1623)
songs.textAuthor: Francis of Assisi (Canticle of the Creatures, 1225); paraphrased by William H. Draper (c. 1919)
songs.about: A free English paraphrase of St. Francis's Canticle of the Creatures, which calls every part of creation to praise God. Popular around the feast of St. Francis (October 4).

songs.title: Let All Mortal Flesh Keep Silence
songs.composer: PICARDY, traditional French carol melody (17th century)
songs.textAuthor: Greek Liturgy of St. James (early centuries); English by Gerard Moultrie (1864)
songs.about: Taken from one of the oldest Eastern liturgies, where it was sung as the gifts were brought to the altar. Its hushed, minor-key melody suits the preparation of the gifts and late Advent.

songs.title: Sing of Mary, Pure and Lowly
songs.composer: PLEADING SAVIOR, from the Plymouth Collection (1855)
songs.about: A gentle hymn on the hidden life of the Holy Family at Nazareth. It suits Marian feasts and the Feast of the Holy Family.

songs.title: Bring Flowers of the Rarest
songs.about: The classic hymn of the May crowning, when a statue of Mary is crowned with flowers. Its authorship is uncertain; it appears in Catholic hymnals from the late 19th century on.

songs.title: Hail, Holy Queen Enthroned Above
songs.composer: SALVE REGINA COELITUM, German melody (Choralmelodien zum Heiligen Gesänge, 1808)
songs.textAuthor: Traditional; English version from The Roman Hymnal (1884)
songs.about: Not a translation of the chant Salve Regina but a separate hymn honoring Mary as Queen, with a festive 'Salve' refrain. It is a frequent closing hymn on Marian feasts.

songs.title: To Jesus Christ, Our Sovereign King
songs.composer: ICH GLAUB AN GOTT, from the Mainz Gesangbuch (1870)
songs.about: Written by a St. Louis pastor and leader of the American liturgical movement for the feast of Christ the King, instituted by Pope Pius XI in 1925. Its refrain is a rousing acclamation of Christ's kingship.

songs.title: Be Thou My Vision
songs.textAuthor: Old Irish poem; translated by Mary E. Byrne (1905) and versified by Eleanor H. Hull (1912)
songs.about: An early Irish prayer asking God to be the center of every part of life. The tune is named for the hill where, by tradition, St. Patrick lit an Easter fire in defiance of the High King.

songs.title: Joyful, Joyful, We Adore Thee
songs.composer: HYMN TO JOY, Ludwig van Beethoven (Symphony No. 9, 1824), adapted by Edward Hodges (1864)
songs.about: An American Presbyterian minister wrote these words for Beethoven's famous 'Ode to Joy' melody. It is a bright, popular hymn for weddings and Easter.

songs.title: Amazing Grace
songs.about: Written by a former slave-ship captain who became an Anglican clergyman, reflecting on his own conversion. Not a liturgical text, but often requested at funerals.

songs.title: Were You There
songs.about: A spiritual that places the singer at the foot of the Cross and at the tomb. It is widely sung on Good Friday and during Lent.

songs.title: Lift High the Cross
songs.textAuthor: George W. Kitchin (1887), revised by Michael R. Newbolt (1916)
songs.about: A processional hymn built for a cross carried at the head of the procession. Especially apt on the Exaltation of the Holy Cross (September 14).

songs.title: O God, Our Help in Ages Past
songs.composer: ST. ANNE, attributed to William Croft (1708)
songs.textAuthor: Isaac Watts (1719), a paraphrase of Psalm 90
songs.about: Watts's paraphrase of Psalm 90 contrasts human frailty with God's eternity. It is often sung at funerals and on national days of remembrance.

songs.title: At the Name of Jesus
songs.about: A hymn on the great Christ-hymn of Philippians 2, in which every knee bends at the name of Jesus. Suited to Palm Sunday and the feast of the Holy Name.

songs.title: Where Charity and Love Prevail
songs.textAuthor: Omer Westendorf (1960), paraphrasing the Latin Ubi caritas
songs.about: A metrical English paraphrase of the chant sung at the washing of feet on Holy Thursday. Also a good fit for weddings and the preparation of the gifts.

songs.title: Hail, Redeemer, King Divine
songs.about: A 20th-century hymn of homage to Christ the King with a march-like refrain. A frequent choice for the last Sunday of the liturgical year.

songs.title: O Lord, I Am Not Worthy
songs.about: A simple traditional communion hymn built on the centurion's words of humility, which the faithful echo just before Communion. Long a fixture of First Communion Masses.

songs.title: Soul of My Savior
songs.composer: ANIMA CHRISTI, William J. Maher, SJ (19th century)
songs.textAuthor: Latin prayer Anima Christi (14th century); English paraphrase anonymous
songs.about: A sung form of the Anima Christi, a medieval prayer after Communion that St. Ignatius of Loyola placed at the start of his Spiritual Exercises.

songs.title: Jesus, My Lord, My God, My All
songs.composer: SWEET SACRAMENT, traditional German melody (19th century)
songs.about: Faber's tender hymn to Christ in the Blessed Sacrament takes its first line from the confession of St. Thomas. A traditional choice for Benediction and Corpus Christi.

songs.title: Good Christian Friends, Rejoice
songs.composer: IN DULCI JUBILO, German melody (14th century)
songs.textAuthor: German-Latin carol (14th century); English by John Mason Neale (1853), altered
songs.about: Neale's version of the medieval carol 'In dulci jubilo,' which mixed Latin and German lines. Older hymnals title it 'Good Christian Men, Rejoice.'

songs.title: The First Noel
songs.composer: THE FIRST NOWELL, traditional English melody
songs.about: A folk carol from the west of England that tells the story of the shepherds and the Magi. It fits Epiphany as well as Christmas Day.

songs.title: O Little Town of Bethlehem
songs.about: Written by a Philadelphia rector after visiting Bethlehem, with music by his church organist. In Britain it is usually sung to Vaughan Williams's FOREST GREEN.

songs.title: Ye Sons and Daughters
songs.composer: O FILII ET FILIAE, French melody (15th century)
songs.textAuthor: Jean Tisserand, OFM (d. 1494); English by John Mason Neale (1851)
songs.about: A narrative Easter hymn that retells the Resurrection appearances, including doubting Thomas. Traditionally associated with the Second Sunday of Easter.

songs.title: Alleluia! Sing to Jesus
songs.about: Written for the feast of the Ascension, it joins Christ's heavenly kingship to his presence in the Eucharist. The Welsh tune HYFRYDOL makes it a strong congregational hymn.

songs.title: Humbly We Adore Thee
songs.composer: ADORO TE DEVOTE, Gregorian chant (Mode V)
songs.about: An English singing version of St. Thomas Aquinas's Adoro Te Devote, sung to its chant melody; the translator varies by hymnal. See the Latin original in this collection.

songs.title: Holy Spirit, Lord of Light
songs.textAuthor: Latin Pentecost Sequence (attributed to Stephen Langton, c. 1200); English by Edward Caswall (1849)
songs.about: Caswall's English version of the Golden Sequence sung before the Gospel on Pentecost Sunday. Webbe was organist at the Sardinian Embassy chapel in London, a hub of Catholic music in penal times.

songs.title: Lo, How a Rose E'er Blooming
songs.composer: ES IST EIN ROS, German melody (Cologne, 1599); harmonized by Michael Praetorius (1609)
songs.textAuthor: German carol (15th–16th century); English by Theodore Baker (1894)
songs.about: A German carol on Isaiah's prophecy of a shoot springing from the stump of Jesse. The Praetorius harmonization is a favorite of choirs in late Advent.

songs.title: At the Cross Her Station Keeping
songs.composer: STABAT MATER, from the Mainz Gesangbuch (1661)
songs.textAuthor: Latin sequence attributed to Jacopone da Todi (13th century); English by Edward Caswall (1849)
songs.about: An English version of the Stabat Mater, traditionally sung verse by verse between the Stations of the Cross. Also used on Our Lady of Sorrows (September 15).

songs.title: All Glory, Laud, and Honor
songs.textAuthor: Theodulf of Orléans (c. 820); English by John Mason Neale (1851)
songs.about: A Palm Sunday processional hymn, said by legend to have been written by a bishop while imprisoned. The Roman Missal names the Latin original among the chants for the Palm Sunday procession.

songs.title: Creator of the Stars of Night
songs.composer: CONDITOR ALME SIDERUM, Gregorian chant (Mode IV)
songs.textAuthor: Latin Office hymn (7th–9th century); English by John Mason Neale (1852), altered
songs.about: The ancient Vespers hymn of Advent, sung to its plainchant melody. Its quiet, flowing line suits the season's spirit of expectation.

songs.title: O Come, Divine Messiah
songs.composer: VENEZ DIVIN MESSIE, French carol melody (16th century)
songs.textAuthor: Simon-Joseph Pellegrin (French, 1708); English by Sister Mary of St. Philip (1877)
songs.about: A French Advent carol of longing for the Savior's coming, translated by an English Sister of Notre Dame. A brighter alternative to the minor-key Advent hymns.

songs.title: Ye Watchers and Ye Holy Ones
songs.composer: LASST UNS ERFREUEN, from Geistliche Kirchengesäng (Cologne, 1623)
songs.about: Calls on the angels, Mary, and all the saints to join in praise; one verse is addressed to the Mother of God. A festive choice for All Saints' Day.

songs.title: For All the Saints
songs.about: A processional hymn giving thanks for the saints who have finished their course. It is a staple of All Saints' Day and is also sung at funerals.

songs.title: Come Down, O Love Divine
songs.textAuthor: Bianco da Siena (Italian, d. 1434); English by Richard F. Littledale (1867)
songs.about: A medieval Italian prayer for the fire of the Holy Spirit, set to a tune Vaughan Williams named after his birthplace. Suits Pentecost and Confirmation.

songs.title: We Three Kings
songs.about: Written for a Christmas pageant in New York, with verses for each gift the Magi bring. Its natural home is the Solemnity of the Epiphany.

songs.title: It Came upon the Midnight Clear
songs.about: An American carol from Massachusetts that dwells on the angels' message of peace to a troubled world.

songs.title: Forty Days and Forty Nights
songs.composer: AUS DER TIEFE (HEINLEIN), from the Nürnbergisches Gesangbuch (1676)
songs.textAuthor: George Hunt Smyttan (1856), altered by Francis Pott
songs.about: A Lenten hymn on Christ's forty days of fasting in the desert, the Gospel of the First Sunday of Lent.

songs.title: Sweet Sacrament Divine
songs.about: A Victorian English Catholic hymn of devotion to the Blessed Sacrament, by a priest who wrote both words and music. Long used at Benediction and Forty Hours.

songs.title: The King of Love My Shepherd Is
songs.textAuthor: Henry W. Baker (1868), a paraphrase of Psalm 23
songs.about: A paraphrase of Psalm 23 that reads the Good Shepherd psalm through the Gospel, including the lost sheep carried home. Fitting at Communion and funerals.

songs.title: Ave Maria (Schubert)
songs.textAuthor: Originally a German song from Walter Scott's 'The Lady of the Lake'; today usually sung to the Latin Ave Maria
songs.about: Schubert's song was written as a maiden's prayer to Mary in a setting of Walter Scott's poem; the familiar Latin words were fitted to it later. A perennial request at weddings and funerals. The Latin prayer itself is under 'Hail Mary (chant)'.

songs.title: Ave Maria (Bach/Gounod)
songs.composer: Charles Gounod (1859), melody laid over J. S. Bach's Prelude in C major (1722)
songs.about: Gounod improvised a soaring melody over the first prelude of Bach's Well-Tempered Clavier, and the Latin Ave Maria was later set to it. Like Schubert's, it is a favorite solo at weddings and funerals.

songs.title: Here I Am, Lord
songs.about: Written for a diaconate ordination, it pairs God's call with the prophet's answer from Isaiah 6. Perhaps the best-known song of the American post-Vatican II repertoire.

songs.title: On Eagle's Wings
songs.about: A paraphrase of Psalm 91 composed by a young Minnesota priest. It is among the most frequently requested songs at Catholic funerals in the United States.

songs.title: Be Not Afraid
songs.about: One of the St. Louis Jesuits' best-known songs, weaving Isaiah 43 together with the Beatitudes in Luke. A frequent choice for funerals.

songs.title: One Bread, One Body
songs.about: A Communion song on St. Paul's teaching that sharing the one loaf makes many into one body. Its simple refrain is easy to sing while processing.

songs.title: You Are Mine
songs.about: A song in the voice of God, built on Isaiah 43's promise of a God who calls each person by name. In 2020 several U.S. dioceses and publishers stopped using or promoting David Haas's music after allegations of misconduct, so check local policy.

songs.title: City of God
songs.about: An upbeat song of mission: the people of God as a light in the darkness. A common sending-forth song.

songs.title: Gather Us In
songs.about: A gathering song about the whole assembly, young and old, rich and poor, called together for worship. Widely used as an opening song.

songs.title: Taste and See
songs.textAuthor: Psalm 34, adapted by James E. Moore Jr.
songs.about: A gospel-flavored setting of Psalm 34, the psalm the early Church sang during Communion. Its call-and-response refrain invites the whole assembly in.

songs.title: Shepherd Me, O God
songs.about: A gentle setting of Psalm 23, the Good Shepherd psalm. It is very common at funerals and at Communion.

songs.title: I Am the Bread of Life
songs.about: Written by a Sister of Mercy in California, its verses come from Jesus' Bread of Life discourse in John 6 and its refrain from his promise of resurrection. A Communion standard for decades.

songs.title: Hosea
songs.about: A song of God calling his people to return, drawn from the prophet Hosea, from the Benedictine monks of Weston Priory in Vermont. A Lenten favorite.

songs.title: Ashes
songs.about: A song closely tied to Ash Wednesday, sung during the distribution of ashes.

songs.title: Lord of the Dance
songs.composer: Sydney Carter, adapted from the Shaker tune SIMPLE GIFTS (Joseph Brackett, 1848)
songs.about: A ballad that retells the life, death, and Resurrection of Christ as a dance, set to the American Shaker tune 'Simple Gifts.' More common at school and youth Masses than at the parish Sunday Mass.

songs.title: Eye Has Not Seen
songs.about: Built on St. Paul's words that no eye has seen what God has prepared for those who love him. A frequent choice at funerals.

songs.title: Prayer of St. Francis (Make Me a Channel of Your Peace)
songs.textAuthor: Sebastian Temple, after the Peace Prayer traditionally attributed to St. Francis
songs.about: A singable version of the 'Peace Prayer,' which first appeared in a French magazine in 1912 and came to be associated with St. Francis. Popular at funerals and on the feast of St. Francis.

songs.title: Pescador de Hombres (Lord, You Have Come)
songs.about: A Spanish song by a Basque priest on Jesus calling fishermen by the lakeshore. It is sung in Spanish, English, and bilingual forms across the United States; it is often said to have been a favorite of St. John Paul II.

songs.title: Sing a New Song
songs.about: A joyful song drawing on the Psalms' call to sing a new song to the Lord. A lively opening or closing song.

songs.title: Christ, Be Our Light
songs.about: A song asking Christ to be light, hope, and bread in a world of darkness and need, by an English composer. Common in Advent and at gatherings with a social-justice theme.

songs.title: Blest Are They
songs.about: A setting of the Beatitudes from the Sermon on the Mount, often sung on All Saints' Day. In 2020 several U.S. dioceses and publishers stopped using or promoting David Haas's music after allegations of misconduct, so check local policy.

songs.title: We Remember
songs.about: A song of trust in God's faithfulness, remembered and renewed. Often sung at Communion.

songs.title: Canticle of the Sun
songs.about: A modern song inspired by St. Francis's Canticle of the Creatures and the Psalms, inviting all creation to praise.

songs.title: The Summons
songs.about: A song of discipleship from the Iona Community in Scotland, cast as a series of questions from Christ to the one he calls. A strong sending-forth song.

songs.title: Let There Be Peace on Earth
songs.about: Written by a husband-and-wife team in California and first taught at a youth retreat. It is a popular closing song, especially at school Masses and civic occasions.

songs.title: How Great Thou Art
songs.textAuthor: Carl Boberg (Swedish, 1885); English by Stuart K. Hine (1949)
songs.about: A Swedish poem of awe at creation, made famous in English through Stuart Hine's translation and the Billy Graham crusades. Frequently requested at funerals.

songs.title: Holy Is His Name
songs.textAuthor: John Michael Talbot, based on the Magnificat
songs.about: A meditative setting of Mary's song of praise, the Magnificat, by the Franciscan musician John Michael Talbot. Fitting on Marian feasts and in late Advent.

songs.title: Mass of Creation
songs.about: For decades the most widely sung Mass setting in American parishes. Haugen revised it in 2010 for the new English translation of the Roman Missal.

songs.title: Mass of Christ the Savior
songs.about: Written for the 2011 introduction of the new English translation of the Roman Missal, it quickly became one of the most used settings in the United States.

songs.title: Mass of Renewal
songs.about: A contemporary Mass setting composed for the current English translation of the Roman Missal, popular with parishes that use contemporary instrumentation.

songs.title: Heritage Mass
songs.about: A simple, sturdy setting that has been a staple of OCP's missalettes, revised in 2010 for the current translation.

songs.title: Mass of St. Ann
songs.about: A singable, contemporary-leaning Mass setting written for the current English translation of the Roman Missal.

songs.title: Mass of Joy and Peace
songs.about: A Mass setting with Latin American rhythmic influences, available in English, Spanish, and bilingual editions.

songs.title: Celtic Alleluia
songs.about: A buoyant Irish Alleluia sung before the Gospel, often with seasonal verses. Because the Alleluia is not sung in Lent, it is set aside from Ash Wednesday until the Easter Vigil.

songs.title: Glory and Praise to Our God
songs.about: A bright gathering song drawn from the Psalms of praise. It gave its name to a widely used hymnal of contemporary Catholic music.

songs.title: Here I Am to Worship
songs.about: A song from the British contemporary worship movement, adopted in many Catholic youth ministries and at Eucharistic adoration.

songs.title: Open My Eyes
songs.about: A prayer to see, hear, and love as Jesus does, with an easy refrain. Popular at youth and school Masses.

songs.title: The Servant Song
songs.about: A song from New Zealand about serving one another as Christ served, often sung at the washing of feet on Holy Thursday.

songs.title: Table of Plenty
songs.about: An invitation to the Lord's table, drawing on Isaiah's banquet imagery.

songs.title: You Satisfy the Hungry Heart (Gift of Finest Wheat)
songs.about: The winning hymn of a competition for the 41st International Eucharistic Congress, held in Philadelphia in 1976. Its title comes from Psalm 81's promise of the finest wheat.

songs.title: We Are Called
songs.about: A sending song built on Micah 6:8: act justly, love tenderly, walk humbly with God. In 2020 several U.S. dioceses and publishers stopped using or promoting David Haas's music after allegations of misconduct, so check local policy.

songs.title: Though the Mountains May Fall
songs.about: A song of confidence in God's unshakable love, from Isaiah 54 and Psalm 46.

songs.title: Come to the Water
songs.about: An invitation from Isaiah 55 to the thirsty and weary to come and be fed freely. Fitting in Lent, especially around the scrutinies.

songs.title: Earthen Vessels
songs.about: From St. Paul's image of carrying the treasure of God's light in clay jars.

songs.title: Sing to the Mountains
songs.about: An exuberant Easter song built on Psalm 118, the psalm of the Easter Octave: this is the day the Lord has made.

songs.title: Lift Up Your Hearts
songs.about: A St. Louis Jesuits gathering song of praise, based on Psalm 66.

songs.title: Sing of the Lord's Goodness
songs.about: A rhythmic, joyful hymn of praise from the English Catholic repertoire, with a jazz-influenced melody.

songs.title: Center of My Life
songs.about: A setting of Psalm 16 with a prayerful refrain naming the Lord as the center of one's life.

songs.title: Holy Darkness
songs.about: A reflective song inspired by St. John of the Cross, finding God present even in the dark night of the soul.

songs.title: Hail Mary: Gentle Woman
songs.about: A tender Marian song that frames the Hail Mary with a sung refrain addressed to Mary. Popular at May crownings and school Masses.

songs.title: Jesus, Remember Me
songs.about: A Taizé chant repeating the good thief's prayer from the Cross. Its short, repeated phrase makes it a natural meditative song for Lent and Good Friday.

songs.title: Ubi Caritas (Taizé)
songs.about: A repetitive Taizé setting of the Holy Thursday antiphon in Latin. The chant original, with a translation, is in this collection under 'Where Charity and Love Are.'

songs.title: Christ Be Beside Me
songs.textAuthor: James Quinn, SJ, adapted from St. Patrick's Breastplate
songs.about: A short adaptation of the prayer known as St. Patrick's Breastplate by a Scottish Jesuit, sung to the same tune as 'Morning Has Broken.' A natural choice for St. Patrick's Day.
